steps.prompt: You roll a die many, many times and write down every number. What do you expect the average of all your numbers to be? Can that average be a number you never roll?

cards.title: The long-run average
cards.body: The expected value is the average result over many tries: multiply each value by its probability and add, $E = \sum (\text{value}) \times P(\text{value})$. It doesn't have to be a value you can actually get.

cards.title: Worked example: one die
cards.problem: What is the expected value of one roll of a fair six-sided die?

cards.title: Expected values add
cards.body: The expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values, even when the parts depend on each other. So the expected total of $n$ dice is $\frac{7n}{2}$, and the expected number of heads in $n$ flips is $\frac{n}{2}$. To count "how many", add up the chance of each single thing happening.

cards.title: Worked example: a spinner
cards.problem: A spinner pays $0$ points with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, $3$ points with probability $\frac{1}{3}$ and $12$ points with probability $\frac{1}{6}$. What is the expected number of points?

try.prompt: What is the expected number of points?

cards.title: The common trap: averaging values that aren't equally likely
cards.body: The spinner's values $0$, $3$ and $12$ average $5$, but the expected value is $3$, because $0$ comes up most often. Weight each value by its probability. In a game, remember to subtract what you pay to play.

prompts: Why can the expected value be a number you can never actually get?
